title: Stop Adding, Start Multiplying
goal: I can use an area model to multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number.

card.desc: Bailey learns the area model: split 75 into 70 + 5, multiply each part by 8, then add (560 + 40 = 600). It replaces her habit of adding 8 over and over, and it runs on the fact shortcuts from Weeks 1 and 2.

win: Two facts and one addition. You just abandoned the slow way!

items.q: A rectangle split into boxes to help you multiply is an area ______.
items.no: Think of the vocabulary card with the purple box.

items.q: Adding 6 + 6 + 6 … ninety times would be slow, hard work. It would be ________.
items.why: Laborious means needing a lot of slow, hard work.
items.no: Which word means slow, hard work?

choices: The immense mouse hid under a leaf.
The immense dragon blocked out the sun.
Hiccup was immense at solving puzzles.
items.why: Immense means extremely large. A dragon big enough to block out the sun is immense.
no: A mouse under a leaf is tiny. Immense means huge.
Immense is about size. Hiccup is clever, which is resourceful.

sets.q: What is 70 × 6?
sets.no: 70 is 7 tens. Do 7 × 6, then keep the zero.

sets.q: Write 58 in expanded form. Type it as ____ + ____ (tens + ones).
This is the area model for 39 × 7. What goes in the 30 box?
sets.no: 30 is 3 tens. Multiply by the side, 7.

sets.q: The partial products for 39 × 7 are 210 and 63. What is 39 × 7?
What is 94 × 9?
Stoick's tribe loads 7 boats. Each boat carries 48 barrels. How many barrels?
The dimensions of a rectangle are …
choices: how long and how wide it is
the answer you get when you add the boxes
sets.why: Dimensions are the measurements of the sides.
no: Boxes are parts. Dimensions are side lengths.
That is the product.
Partial products are the answers inside the boxes. Dimensions are the side lengths.

sets.q: Which way finds 86 × 6 with the fewest steps and the right answer?
sets.why: 480 + 36 = 516 with two facts and one addition.
no: Correct, but 86 numbers to add is laborious and easy to mess up.
The 6 box must be multiplied: 6 × 6 = 36.

sets.q: To abandon a plan means to …
choices: stop using it and leave it behind
sets.why: Abandon means to leave something behind.
no: That is the opposite of abandon.
Abandon means to leave it.
Sharing keeps the plan. Abandon means leave it.

sets.q: The sea dragon was so immense that …
choices: the Viking ship looked tiny next to it
it came up with a clever trick
no: Immense means huge, not tiny.
A clever trick shows someone is resourceful, not immense.

sets.q: What is 90 × 8?
sets.no: 90 is 9 tens. Do 9 × 8, then keep the zero.

sets.q: Write 73 in expanded form. Type it as ____ + ____ (tens + ones).
This is the area model for 56 × 9. What goes in the 50 box?
sets.no: 50 is 5 tens. Multiply by the side, 9.

sets.q: The partial products for 56 × 9 are 450 and 54. What is 56 × 9?
sets.no: Add the two partial products. 5 tens + 5 tens = 10 tens.

sets.q: What is 87 × 7?
Gobber sharpens 65 swords a week. How many swords does he sharpen in 8 weeks?
In the area model for 84 × 6, the dimensions of the rectangle are …
sets.why: The dimensions are the side lengths: 84 and 6.
no: 80 and 4 are the parts of 84. Dimensions are the whole side lengths.
Those are the partial products inside the boxes.
504 is the final product, not a side length.

sets.q: Which way finds 79 × 8 with the fewest steps and the right answer?
no: That is laborious: 79 numbers to add, and one slip ruins it.
The 9 box must be multiplied by 8 too: 9 × 8 = 72.
That is adding, not multiplying.

sets.q: Something that is laborious …
choices: takes a lot of slow, hard work
is done in one quick step
sets.why: Laborious means needing a lot of slow, hard work.
no: That is immense.
That is the opposite of laborious.
Laborious is about slow, hard work, not tricks.

sets.q: Hiccup is not strong enough to win a fight, so he uses his brain and a clever plan. Which word describes him?
sets.why: Resourceful means good at finding clever ways to solve a problem with what you have.
no: Immense means huge. Hiccup is small but clever.
Laborious describes slow, hard work, not a person who finds clever ways.
Abandoned means left behind.

sets.q: What is 50 × 7?
sets.no: 50 is 5 tens. Do 5 × 7, then keep the zero.

sets.q: Write 92 in expanded form. Type it as ____ + ____ (tens + ones).
This is the area model for 76 × 6. What goes in the 70 box?
sets.no: 70 is 7 tens. Multiply by the side, 6.

sets.q: The partial products for 76 × 6 are 420 and 36. What is 76 × 6?
What is 59 × 8?
Each Viking longhouse has 34 beds. There are 9 longhouses. How many beds?
Which word names the answer from one box of an area model?
no: Dimensions are the side lengths.
Expanded form splits a number into tens and ones, like 70 + 6.
The final product comes from adding all the boxes.

sets.q: Which plan finds 35 × 9 correctly?
no: The 5 box must be multiplied by 9 too.
The 3 in 35 is 3 tens: use 30 × 9.
That is adding, not multiplying.

sets.q: Hiccup decides to abandon his old plan. What does he do?
choices: He follows it step by step.
He stops using it and leaves it behind.
sets.why: Abandon means to leave something behind and stop using it.
no: That is the opposite of abandon.
Telling someone keeps the plan. Abandon means leave it.
Abandon means to stop using it.

sets.q: The dragon was so immense that …
choices: it could sleep in a teacup
its shadow covered the whole village
no: Immense means huge, not tiny.
Only a tiny dragon fits in a pocket.
Solving puzzles is clever, not immense.

You could do it. It would just take forever.
That is immense.

teacher.objective: Bailey multiplies a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number with a two-box area model (75 × 8 = 70 × 8 + 5 × 8) and can explain why it beats adding 8 seventy-five times. This is the direct fix for her habit of adding a number over and over.
materials: Zoom with screen share of the Class Lesson (teacher code 9110)
At home: her whiteboard (or paper) and a marker to hold up to the camera
At home: 3 cups and about 50 dry beans (for the 'Why splitting works' slide)
At home: grid paper and 2 colored pencils
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Packet (2 pages): assigned on Tuesday's task list, so it does not need to be printed today

plan.do: Class slide 1. She holds up each item to the camera. Ask for her guess: is 75 × 8 closer to 60, 600 or 6,000?
Class slide 2. She retells in order. Push on prompt 2: Hiccup wins with brains, not muscle. Tie it to today: math brains (multiplying) beat math muscle (adding).
Class slide 3. She tells you which card to flip, reads each aloud and makes her own sentence with laborious, immense and abandon.
Class slide 4. 30-second timer: she writes 8 + 8 + 8 … with a running total. Stop and discuss how far 75 eights would take.
Class slides 5–6. 7 tens × 8 = 56 tens = 560 on her whiteboard. She says each tens fact aloud before telling you her choice.
Class slide 7. 3 cups of 14 beans; she splits each cup into 10 and 4 and counts 30 + 12 = 42.
Class slide 8. She draws 75 × 8 on grid paper (two colors), writes 560 and 40 inside, adds to 600 and compares to her guess.

plan.block: Fill the boxes + order the steps
plan.do: Class slides 9–10. 46 × 7 on paper before she picks an answer; she says each step of 57 × 8 aloud.
Class slide 11. She teaches you 38 × 9 box by box, whiteboard up after each box.
Class slide 12. She draws the area model for each story before she picks an answer.
Class slide 13. She names the shortcut (×9, ×8, ×6) before she picks an answer.
Class slide 14. She explains why each wrong choice is wrong.
Class slide 15 on her own: 63 × 7 and the partial-product word. No hints.
Class slide 16. She says the three steps from memory. Show the course page: tonight is only the After-Class Lesson (ends with Show What You Know) and 10 minutes of reading.

watch: Dropping the zero (70 × 8 = 56). Ask: is 70 a ones number or a tens number? Say it as 7 tens × 8 = 56 tens.
Adding the factors (75 + 8 = 83) when she rushes. Ask: are there 8 equal groups of 75? Then multiply.
Multiplying only the tens box and writing the ones digit (560 + 5 = 565). Point to the ones box: it is a rectangle too, so it gets multiplied.
Missing regrouping when adding partial products (280 + 42 = 312). Have her add tens to tens out loud.
"I can't do it." Point to the rectangle: it is only two facts she already knows. Have her do one box at a time.

packet_key.answer: area model → a rectangle split into boxes to multiply; partial product → the answer from one box; expanded form → a number written as tens + ones; laborious → needing a lot of slow, hard work; resourceful → good at finding clever ways to solve problems; abandon → to leave behind and stop using
Two complete sentences that use resourceful (clever at solving problems) or immense (huge) correctly about something in the book, with a reason.

teacher.notes: Tonight she does the After-Class Lesson on her own; it ends with Show What You Know (3 different question sets for retakes; she needs 90). Lesson 7 is tomorrow in person, so check the Formspree score before class. If she is under 90, start Lesson 7 with 10 minutes of two-box area models on grid paper (for example 57 × 9 and 82 × 6) and have her retake the check (she gets a new set). If tens facts are the problem, drill 5 of them aloud (60 × 8, 70 × 9 …) before any area model. Lesson 6's practice set and packet are assigned on Tuesday's task list.

slides.title: Stop Adding, Start Multiplying
slides.text: Your 6, 7, 8 and 9 facts are getting fast. Today they become power tools for big problems like 75 × 8. Have your whiteboard, grid paper, 2 colored pencils, 3 cups and about 50 dry beans ready.

visual.sub: No more adding 8 over and over!

notes.do: Screen-share this slide on Zoom. Before you start, have her hold up each item to the camera: whiteboard and marker, grid paper, 2 colored pencils, 3 cups, about 50 dry beans, and her book.
notes.say: Today we are going to stop doing something slow and start doing something smart. By the end of class you will find 75 × 8 with just two facts and one addition.
notes.ask: Without working it out, do you think 75 × 8 is closer to 60, 600 or 6,000?
notes.listen: Right: about 600 (75 is close to 80, and 80 × 8 = 640). If she says 60 or 6,000, do not correct yet; say: hold on to that guess and we will check it.

slides.title: Brains or muscles?
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: What happened in the part you read last? Tell it in order: first, next, then.
Hiccup is not the biggest or strongest Viking on Berk. What does he use instead to solve problems?
Find a time someone in the book did something the hard way. What would have been a smarter way?
starters: In the part I read, first …
A smarter way would be … because …

notes.do: 5–6 minutes. She talks; you only ask follow-ups. Tap the gold star button for a strong, detailed answer.
notes.say: Tell me what happened in the part you read, in order. Use first, next, then.
notes.ask: Hiccup is not the strongest Viking. So what does he use to win? Can you think of a time someone in the book did something the hard way?
notes.listen: A strong answer names a real event and uses a sequence word. For prompt 2 listen for brains, ideas, tricks, planning. Connect it: today we stop using math muscles (adding 8 over and over) and start using math brains (multiplying).

slides.title: Words for today
slides.text: Flip each card. Read the word, the meaning and the example out loud.

words.meaning: A rectangle split into boxes that helps you multiply a big number one part at a time.
words.example: I drew an area model for 75 × 8 with two boxes.

words.meaning: The answer from one box of an area model. You add the partial products to get the final answer.
A number written as the sum of the values of its digits.
The measurements of the sides of a shape: how long and how wide it is.
words.example: The dimensions of my rectangle are 75 and 8.

words.meaning: Needing a lot of slow, hard work.
Good at finding clever ways to solve a problem with what you have.
words.example: Hiccup cannot win with muscles, so he has to be resourceful.
Next to an immense sea dragon, a Viking ship looks like a toy.

words.meaning: To leave something behind and stop using it.
words.example: Today we abandon the slow adding method.

notes.do: She tells you which card to flip (on Zoom she cannot tap your screen), then reads the word, meaning and example aloud. After each book word (laborious, resourceful, immense, abandon), she makes her own sentence.
notes.say: Four of these words are math words we will use all class. Four are strong words for your book and your writing.
notes.ask: Use laborious in a sentence about chores. Use immense in a sentence about a dragon. What is something you would abandon if it was not working?
notes.listen: Laborious = slow, hard work (not just hard). Immense = huge. If she says 'immense means scary', ask: could a tiny spider be immense? No, so immense is about size.

slides.title: Why adding is so slow
slides.text: The old way to find 75 × 8: add 8 again and again.

steps.text: That is 75 numbers to add. If you lose count once, the answer is wrong.
It is laborious, and it hides how big the answer really is.
Today you abandon that method. You will use just two facts and one addition.

slides.tip: Multiplying is a shortcut for adding equal groups. Big numbers need a smart shortcut too.

notes.do: Hands-on race first: start a 30-second timer and have her write 8 + 8 + 8 + … on her whiteboard and keep a running total. Stop her at 30 seconds.
notes.say: Stop! How many eights did you get through? To find 75 × 8 that way you would need 75 of them, with no mistakes.
notes.ask: If you lose count at the 40th eight, what happens to your answer? Why is this method laborious?
notes.listen: She should say the answer would be wrong and it takes too long. Then click through the 3 steps and have her read them aloud.

slides.title: Facts with a zero
slides.text: You know 7 × 8 = 56. So what is 70 × 8?
slides.tip: Do the fact first. Then keep the zero: tens times a number still gives tens.

notes.do: Click through the steps one at a time. Have her write 7 tens × 8 = 56 tens on her whiteboard and hold it up.
notes.say: 70 is not seventy ones. It is 7 tens. 7 tens times 8 is 56 tens. 56 tens is 560.
notes.ask: If 6 × 9 = 54, what is 60 × 9? How many zeros does the answer get, and why?
notes.listen: Right: 540, one zero because only one factor is a tens number. Wrong: 54 (dropped the zero) or 5,400 (too many zeros). Say it again in tens: 6 tens × 9 = 54 tens.

no: That is 6 × 7. But 60 is 6 tens, so the answer is 42 tens.
Too many zeros. Only one factor has a zero, so the answer gets one zero.
You wrote the digits side by side. Multiply 6 × 7 first.
You added 90 + 6. The sign says multiply.
That is 90 × 5. One more group of 90 makes 540.
Too many zeros. 9 × 6 = 54, and 90 has one zero.

items.q: Which one shows how to find 80 × 9?
no: That is adding. You need the fact 8 × 9.
Only one zero. 80 has one zero, so the answer has one more zero than 72.

notes.do: She says each fact in tens out loud, then tells you which answer to tap. Example: '6 tens times 7 is 42 tens, so 420.'
notes.ask: Before you pick: what is the basic fact hiding in this problem?
notes.listen: If she picks 42 or 4,200, have her say the tens sentence and try again. The third item is about reasoning: ask why 7,200 has one zero too many.

slides.title: Why splitting works
slides.text: Put 14 beans in each of 3 cups. That is 3 × 14.

visual.label: 3 cups of 14 beans (one row for each cup)

steps.text: In each cup, split the beans into a pile of 10 and a pile of 4.
30 + 12 = 42. Splitting did not change the beans. It just made them easier to count.

slides.tip: That is exactly what an area model does: split the big number, multiply each part, add.

notes.do: At home on camera: she counts 14 beans into each of the 3 cups. Then she pours each cup out and pushes the beans into a pile of 10 and a pile of 4. Click the steps as she does it.
notes.say: We did not add or remove a single bean. We only split each group into tens and ones. Splitting makes the counting easy.
notes.ask: How many beans are in all the 10-piles together? In all the 4-piles? So how many beans in all?
notes.listen: 30, 12, 42. If she starts counting beans one by one, stop her: use the fact 3 × 10 and the fact 3 × 4.

slides.title: Meet the area model
slides.text: Let's find 75 × 8 with an area model.

steps.text: Step 2. Draw a rectangle. Split it into a 70 box and a 5 box. The other side is 8.
Step 3. Multiply each box. 70 × 8 = 560 and 5 × 8 = 40. These are the partial products.

slides.tip: Two facts (7 × 8 and 5 × 8) and one addition. That beats 75 additions!

notes.do: Click one step at a time. At step 2, she draws a long rectangle on grid paper, colors the 70 part one color and the 5 part another, and holds it up to the camera.
notes.say: Step 1: expanded form. Step 2: draw the boxes. Step 3: multiply each box. Step 4: add. That is two facts and one addition instead of 75 additions.
notes.ask: Why is the 70 box so much bigger than the 5 box? Which basic fact do you need for each box? Now look back: was your guess of 600 from the start of class right?
notes.listen: She should say 7 × 8 and 5 × 8. The 70 box is bigger because 70 is bigger than 5. 560 + 40 = 600 matches the guess from slide 1.

items.q: This is the area model for 46 × 7. What goes in the 40 box?
no: You added 40 + 7. Each box is multiplied.
That is 40 × 6. The side of the rectangle is 7, so do 40 × 7.

items.q: The partial products for 46 × 7 are 280 and 42. What is 46 × 7?
no: Check the addition: 280 + 40 = 320, and 2 more is 322.
You added 28 + 42, but the 40 box holds 280, not 28.

items.q: Which area model is set up correctly for 83 × 6?
items.why: 83 = 80 + 3, and the side of the rectangle is 6.
no: The 8 in 83 is really 80. Use expanded form: 80 + 3.
Split 83 into 80 + 3. The 6 is the other side of the rectangle.

notes.do: She draws the 46 × 7 rectangle on her paper and writes the partial products inside BEFORE she tells you which answer to tap.
notes.ask: What goes in the 40 box? What goes in the 6 box? Now add them.
notes.listen: 280 and 42, total 322. If she says 240 she multiplied by 6 instead of 7: point to the side of the rectangle. For item 3 she must say why 8 and 3 is wrong (the 8 is really 80).

slides.title: Area model steps: 57 × 8
slides.text: Tap the steps in the order you would do them.
steps: Draw a 50 box and a 7 box with side 8
slides.hint: Start by breaking 57 into tens and ones. You need the boxes before you can multiply them, and the partial products before you can add.

notes.do: She reads each step aloud and tells you which one to tap next.
notes.ask: Why can't you add the partial products before you multiply the boxes?
notes.listen: Because you need the boxes before you can multiply them, and the partial products before you can add. Answer: 456.

slides.title: Your turn, out loud: 38 × 9
slides.text: Draw it on your whiteboard first. Tell me each box, and I will type what you say.

items.no: 30 is 3 tens. Do 3 × 9, then keep the zero.
Multiply 8 by the side of the rectangle, 9.

notes.do: She leads this one. You only ask the questions. Her whiteboard goes up to the camera after each box.
notes.say: You are the teacher now. Tell me every step.
notes.ask: What is 38 in expanded form? Which side is the 9 on? Which fact gives the 8 box?
notes.listen: She should say 30 + 8, then 270, then 72, then 342. If she freezes on 8 × 9, ask: what is ten 8s? Take away one 8.

items.q: Gobber hangs 8 rows of shields in the Great Hall. Each row has 36 shields. How many shields?
no: You added 36 + 8. There are 8 equal rows of 36, so multiply.
The tens box is right (240), but the ones box is 6 × 8 = 48, not 8.

items.q: Fishlegs wants to find 64 × 9. Which way is fast and correct?
no: That works, but it is laborious: 64 numbers to add, and one slip ruins it.
The 4 box must be multiplied by 9 too: 4 × 9 = 36.
That is adding, not multiplying.

notes.do: For each story she draws the area model on her whiteboard first, then tells you which answer to tap.
notes.ask: What are the equal groups in this story? How many groups, and how many in each?
notes.listen: 8 rows of 36 shields. If she adds 36 + 8, ask: are there 8 equal rows? Then it is multiplication. For Fishlegs, she must say why the other ways are slow or wrong.

slides.title: Your fact shortcuts
slides.text: These shortcuts from the last two weeks make the boxes fast.

no: Nine groups is one group less than ten groups, so subtract.
That is 9 × 9. Take away one group of 8, not 9.
42 is 28 + 14. Doubling 28 means 28 + 28.

items.q: 6 × 7 is 5 × 7 plus one more group. Which is right?
no: One more group of 7, not 6.
Add one whole group of 7, not just 1.

notes.do: Quick and out loud. She names the shortcut before she tells you her choice.
notes.say: Every box in an area model needs a fact. These shortcuts make the boxes fast.
notes.ask: Which shortcut works for 9s? For 8s? For 6s?
notes.listen: 9s: ten groups minus one group. 8s: double, double, double. 6s: five groups plus one group.

choices: The race was so laborious that it ended in two seconds.
Toothless gave a laborious roar that made everyone jump.
Counting 600 grains of sand one by one is laborious.
items.why: Counting one by one is slow, hard work. That is laborious.
no: Laborious means slow, hard work. A two-second race is the opposite.
A roar that makes people jump is loud or fierce, not slow, hard work.
An answer is not slow, hard work. The adding method is laborious.

items.q: In the area model for 75 × 8, which numbers are the partial products?
no: Those are the parts of 75 in expanded form. Partial products come from multiplying.
600 is the final product. The partial products are the pieces you add to get it.
Those are the dimensions of the rectangle.

items.q: Hiccup cannot beat a huge dragon with muscles, so he finds a clever way with what he has. Which word describes Hiccup?
items.why: Resourceful means good at finding clever ways to solve a problem with what you have.
no: Immense means huge. Hiccup is not huge; he is clever.
Laborious describes slow, hard work, not a clever person.
Abandoned means left behind. Hiccup is not left behind.

notes.do: Before she gives her choice, she reads every choice out loud and says why the wrong ones are wrong.
notes.ask: Why is 'the laborious answer is 600' a wrong use of the word?
notes.listen: An answer is not slow, hard work; the adding method is. For the partial products item, she must say 560 and 40 come from multiplying the boxes.

slides.title: Check for understanding
slides.text: On your own. Work on your whiteboard, hold it up, then tell me what to enter.

items.no: Split 63 into 60 + 3. Multiply each part by 7.

items.q: The two answers inside the boxes of an area model are called …
items.why: Each box gives a partial product. You add them to get the final product.
no: Dimensions are the side lengths of the rectangle, like 63 and 7.
Expanded form is 60 + 3: the parts of the number before you multiply.

notes.say: This one is just to show me what you know. No hints from me.
notes.listen: 441 with no help means she is ready for the after-class lesson tonight. If she writes 42 + 21 = 63, she dropped the zero: re-teach slide 5 for one minute and give her 52 × 8 (400 + 16 = 416).

slides.title: What you can do now
slides.text: You can multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number without adding over and over.

steps.text: 1. Split the big number in expanded form: 75 = 70 + 5.
2. Multiply each box. Do the fact, then keep the zero: 560 and 40.
Tonight: the After-Class Lesson on your own (it ends with Show What You Know), then read for 10 minutes. That is all!

slides.tip: Two facts and one addition beat 75 additions every time.
